stem: A 58-year-old man in Peshawar presents with chest pain. ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF, and soon afterwards complete heart block develops. Occlusion of which artery best explains both the infarct and the conduction block?
explanation: Leads II, III and aVF face the inferior wall, which in most people is supplied by the right coronary artery; in a right-dominant circulation the RCA also gives the artery to the AV node, so heart block commonly accompanies inferior infarction. The circumflex artery supplies the lateral wall and only supplies the AV node in a left-dominant circulation.

stem: A 50-year-old smoker has an anterior myocardial infarction with ST elevation in leads V1 to V4. Which artery is most likely occluded?
explanation: The left anterior descending artery runs in the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the anterior left ventricle and the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum, which leads V1 to V4 face. The posterior descending artery supplies the inferior wall and posterior septum.

stem: During coronary bypass surgery, the surgeon passes a finger behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk and in front of the superior vena cava and pulmonary veins, so that a clamp can be placed across the great arteries. Into which space has the finger been passed?
explanation: The transverse pericardial sinus is the passage within the serous pericardium between the arterial outflow (aorta and pulmonary trunk) in front and the venous inflow (SVC and pulmonary veins) behind. The oblique sinus is a blind recess behind the left atrium, bounded by the pulmonary veins and IVC, and a finger cannot pass through it.

stem: A 62-year-old man has crushing central chest pain that radiates down the inner side of his left arm. What best explains the pain being felt in the medial arm?
options: The phrenic nerve supplies both the pericardium and the skin of the medial arm
The vagus nerve carries pain from the heart to the brachial plexus
Ischaemia spreads to the axillary lymph nodes
Cardiac pain fibres enter the same spinal segments as medial arm skin
explanation: Visceral pain fibres from the heart travel with sympathetic nerves to the T1–T4 segments, which also receive somatic sensation from the medial arm (T1–T2, partly via the intercostobrachial nerve); the brain misattributes the pain to the skin. Vagal afferents mainly carry reflex and stretch information, not cardiac pain, and the phrenic nerve explains shoulder-tip, not medial arm, pain.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatic mitral stenosis has difficulty swallowing solids and a hoarse voice. Enlargement of which cardiac chamber is most likely responsible?
explanation: The left atrium forms most of the posterior surface (base) of the heart and lies directly in front of the oesophagus; in mitral stenosis it enlarges and can compress the oesophagus and, rarely, the left recurrent laryngeal nerve (Ortner's syndrome). The right ventricle forms most of the anterior surface and does not contact the oesophagus.

stem: A final-year student is examining a patient with a mid-diastolic rumble. Where on the chest wall are sounds from the mitral valve best heard?
options: Right second intercostal space at the right sternal edge
Left second intercostal space at the sternal edge
Left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line
explanation: Mitral valve sounds are best heard at the apex, usually in the left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line, where blood flow carries the sound. The lower left sternal edge is the tricuspid area, and the second spaces are the aortic (right) and pulmonary (left) areas.

stem: A 16-year-old boy has hypertension in his arms and weak, delayed femoral pulses. His chest X-ray shows notching of the inferior borders of the posterior ribs. Enlargement of which vessels causes the rib notching?
explanation: In coarctation of the aorta, blood bypasses the narrowing via the subclavian and internal thoracic arteries into the intercostal arteries, which fill the posterior intercostal arteries in reverse to reach the descending aorta. These dilated, tortuous arteries in the costal grooves erode the lower rib borders. The internal thoracic and superior epigastric arteries are part of the collateral pathway but do not lie against the ribs posteriorly.

stem: A 6-month-old boy has cyanotic spells, a harsh systolic murmur, and a boot-shaped heart on chest X-ray. Which single embryological error underlies the four features of this condition?
options: Failure of the endocardial cushions to fuse
Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to follow a spiral course
Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular (outlet) septum
Persistence of the right sixth pharyngeal arch artery
explanation: In tetralogy of Fallot, anterosuperior deviation of the infundibular septum narrows the right ventricular outflow (pulmonary stenosis), leaves a ventricular septal defect, and lets the aorta override the septum; right ventricular hypertrophy follows. Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral causes transposition of the great arteries instead.

stem: A preterm baby girl born to a mother who had rubella in early pregnancy has a continuous 'machinery' murmur below the left clavicle. The vessel that has failed to close develops from which embryological structure?
explanation: The ductus arteriosus is formed from the distal part of the left sixth pharyngeal arch artery and connects the pulmonary trunk to the aortic arch; a patent ductus causes a continuous machinery murmur and is linked with prematurity and congenital rubella. The left fourth arch artery forms part of the aortic arch.

stem: Within minutes of birth, the foramen ovale closes functionally. Which change is mainly responsible?
options: Left atrial pressure becomes higher than right atrial pressure
Contraction of muscle in the septum primum
Rising circulating prostaglandin levels after the placenta separates
Increased blood flow through the ductus venosus
explanation: With the first breaths, pulmonary resistance falls and pulmonary venous return increases left atrial pressure, while loss of placental flow reduces right atrial pressure; the septum primum is pushed against the septum secundum, closing the foramen ovale. Prostaglandin levels fall, not rise, after birth, which helps the ductus arteriosus close.

stem: A 28-year-old man with acute pericarditis has sharp chest pain that is also felt at the tip of his left shoulder. Which nerve carries the pain that is referred to the shoulder tip?
explanation: The fibrous and parietal serous pericardium receive sensory fibres from the phrenic nerve (C3–C5); C4 also supplies the skin over the shoulder through the supraclavicular nerves, so pericardial pain is referred there. The intercostobrachial nerve supplies the medial arm and axilla, not the shoulder tip.

stem: A 3-year-old boy in Hyderabad starts coughing and wheezing after choking on a peanut. Into which bronchus is the peanut most likely to have lodged?
explanation: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, so inhaled foreign bodies usually pass into it. The left main bronchus leaves the trachea at a more horizontal angle, passing under the aortic arch.

stem: A 50-year-old man is found unconscious lying on his back after a seizure. A week later he has fever and a cough, and imaging shows an aspiration pneumonia. Which bronchopulmonary segment is most likely to be involved?
options: Superior (apical) segment of the right lower lobe
Medial segment of the middle lobe of the right lung
Anterior segment of the right upper lobe
Lingular segment of the left upper lobe
explanation: In a supine patient the superior segment of the lower lobe is the most dependent, because its bronchus arises posteriorly, and the right side is favoured because the right main bronchus is more vertical. In upright patients aspiration goes to the basal segments of the right lower lobe instead. The anterior and middle lobe segments arise anteriorly and are not dependent when lying on the back.

stem: A house officer is inserting a chest drain in a man with a traumatic haemothorax. Why should the needle and drain pass just above the upper border of the rib below?
options: The intercostal muscles are absent there
The long thoracic nerve runs along the lower border of each rib in the chest wall
The neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove of the rib above
explanation: The main intercostal neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve from above down) runs in the costal groove on the inferior border of each rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles. Passing just above the lower rib avoids it; only small collateral branches lie there. The long thoracic nerve runs on the outer surface of serratus anterior, not in the intercostal space.

stem: A 22-year-old man with a large spontaneous pneumothorax needs a chest drain. In which site is the drain normally inserted in the 'safe triangle'?
options: Second intercostal space in the midclavicular line
Seventh intercostal space in the scapular line
Fifth intercostal space just anterior to the midaxillary line
Ninth intercostal space in the posterior axillary line, below the scapula
explanation: The safe triangle is bounded by the lateral border of pectoralis major, the anterior border of latissimus dorsi and a horizontal line at the level of the nipple (about the fifth intercostal space); a drain in the fifth space just anterior to the midaxillary line avoids the internal thoracic vessels, the long thoracic nerve and the diaphragm. The second space in the midclavicular line is used for needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax in some protocols, not routine drains.

stem: A surgeon is making a posterior incision below the right 12th rib to approach the kidney. Which structure is at risk of being opened near the medial end of the incision, leading to a pneumothorax?
options: Inferior border of the lower lobe of the right lung
explanation: Posteriorly, the parietal pleura extends down to about the level of the 12th rib and may project below its medial part at the costovertebral angle, so the costodiaphragmatic recess can be opened in a subcostal loin incision. The lung itself does not extend that low; its lower border lies about two ribs higher than the pleura.

stem: A 65-year-old smoker has pain in the shoulder and along the inner side of his right arm, wasting of the small muscles of the right hand, and a small right pupil with ptosis. Chest X-ray shows a mass at the right lung apex. Which structure compressed by the tumour causes the eye signs?
options: Cervical sympathetic chain and stellate ganglion
Right recurrent laryngeal nerve where it loops around the subclavian artery
explanation: An apical (Pancoast) tumour invades the lower brachial plexus (C8, T1), causing arm pain and hand wasting, and the cervicothoracic (stellate) sympathetic ganglion on the neck of the first rib, causing Horner's syndrome. Recurrent laryngeal involvement would cause hoarseness, not ptosis and miosis.

stem: At which vertebral level does the oesophagus pass through the diaphragm, accompanied by the vagal trunks?
explanation: The oesophageal hiatus lies at about T10 in the muscular right crus and transmits the oesophagus, the anterior and posterior vagal trunks and oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels. The IVC passes through the central tendon at T8, and the aorta passes behind the median arcuate ligament at T12.

stem: A newborn in a tertiary hospital in Karachi has respiratory distress, a scaphoid abdomen and bowel sounds heard in the left chest. Through which defect has the abdominal content most likely herniated?
options: Anterior retrosternal defect beside the xiphoid process
Posterolateral defect of the left hemidiaphragm
explanation: Most congenital diaphragmatic hernias (Bochdalek type) pass through a posterolateral defect, usually on the left, from failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close; the herniated gut compresses the developing lung, causing pulmonary hypoplasia. An anterior (Morgagni) retrosternal defect is much less common and often asymptomatic in the newborn.

stem: After a left-sided neck dissection for lymphoma biopsy, milky fluid leaks from the wound at the root of the neck. Which structure has most likely been damaged?
explanation: The thoracic duct ascends through the thorax, crosses from right to left at about T5 and ends in the left venous angle at the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins, so it is at risk in left neck surgery and leaks milky chyle. The right lymphatic duct drains into the right venous angle, and the cisterna chyli lies in the abdomen.

stem: At operation on a 25-year-old man with a right inguinal hernia, the surgeon finds that the sac passes through the deep inguinal ring and lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. What type of hernia is this?
explanation: An indirect inguinal hernia enters the canal through the deep ring, which lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, and follows the spermatic cord, often as a remnant of the processus vaginalis. A direct hernia pushes through the posterior wall medial to these vessels in the inguinal (Hesselbach's) triangle.

stem: A 68-year-old man who has had a chronic cough has a reducible bulge in the groin. At surgery the hernia passes through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal medial to the inferior epigastric artery. Which structure forms the medial boundary of the triangle through which this hernia passes?
explanation: This direct hernia passes through the inguinal (Hesselbach's) triangle, bounded medially by the lateral border of rectus abdominis, laterally by the inferior epigastric artery and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament. The lacunar ligament forms the medial boundary of the femoral ring, not of this triangle.

stem: A 70-year-old woman has a tender, irreducible lump in the groin below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, with vomiting and distension. The surgeon notes that the neck of the sac is tight because its medial boundary is a sharp, unyielding ligament. Which ligament is this?
explanation: A femoral hernia passes through the femoral ring, bounded medially by the sharp lacunar ligament, anteriorly by the inguinal ligament, posteriorly by the pectineal ligament and laterally by the femoral vein. The rigid medial edge explains why femoral hernias strangulate readily and may need the lacunar ligament to be incised.

stem: Three months after an open inguinal hernia repair, a 40-year-old man complains of numbness over the root of the penis and the front of the scrotum, with burning pain in the groin. Which nerve was most likely injured?
options: Femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve
Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
explanation: The ilioinguinal nerve (L1) runs through the inguinal canal in front of the spermatic cord and emerges through the superficial ring to supply the root of the penis, anterior scrotum and upper medial thigh, so it is vulnerable during open repair. The iliohypogastric nerve supplies the suprapubic skin, and the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies skin over the femoral triangle.

stem: A paediatrician strokes the upper medial thigh of a 6-year-old boy and the ipsilateral testis rises. Which nerve carries the motor limb of this reflex?
options: Anterior scrotal branches of the ilioinguinal nerve
Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve
explanation: The cremasteric reflex (L1–L2) has its sensory limb mainly in the femoral branch of the genitofemoral and the ilioinguinal nerves, and its motor limb in the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, which supplies cremaster. The ilioinguinal nerve is sensory to this area and does not supply cremaster.

stem: During insertion of a lateral laparoscopic port in the lower abdomen, brisk bleeding occurs from the abdominal wall, and later a haematoma forms within the rectus sheath. Which vessel was most likely injured?
explanation: The inferior epigastric artery arises from the external iliac artery, runs upwards behind rectus abdominis inside the rectus sheath and can be injured by ports placed near the lateral border of rectus; bleeding forms a rectus sheath haematoma. Superficial vessels lie in subcutaneous tissue and do not bleed into the sheath.

stem: A 45-year-old man with known peptic ulcer disease presents with haematemesis and melaena. Endoscopy shows a bleeding ulcer in the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum. Which artery is most likely eroded?
explanation: The gastroduodenal artery descends directly behind the first part of the duodenum, so a posterior duodenal ulcer can erode it and cause major bleeding. The left gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature and bleeds from lesser curve gastric ulcers; the splenic artery lies behind the stomach along the upper border of the pancreas.

stem: A 19-year-old student has central abdominal pain around the umbilicus that, 12 hours later, shifts to the right iliac fossa. What explains the initial periumbilical location of the pain?
options: Visceral afferents from the appendix enter the T10 spinal segment
The appendix lies behind the umbilicus in most people
The ilioinguinal nerve supplies the parietal peritoneum at the umbilicus
Inflammation first spreads to the umbilical lymph nodes
explanation: The appendix is a midgut derivative, and its visceral pain fibres travel with sympathetic nerves to about the T10 segment, so early, poorly localised pain is referred to the T10 dermatome around the umbilicus. Once the parietal peritoneum in the right iliac fossa is inflamed, somatic nerves localise the pain there.

stem: During laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the surgeon dissects the triangle bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the inferior surface of the liver. Which artery is usually found in this triangle and must be clipped?
explanation: The cystic artery usually arises from the right hepatic artery within the hepatobiliary (Calot's) triangle and is clipped there. The right hepatic artery may also pass through the triangle and is at risk of being mistaken for it, but the gastroduodenal and right gastric arteries arise from the common hepatic artery outside the triangle.

stem: During laparotomy for a liver laceration after a road traffic accident, the surgeon compresses the free edge of the lesser omentum between finger and thumb, but dark blood continues to well up from behind the liver. Which vessels are most likely bleeding?
options: Hepatic veins or retrohepatic inferior vena cava
Branches of the proper hepatic artery
explanation: Compressing the hepatoduodenal ligament (Pringle manoeuvre) occludes the hepatic artery and portal vein, so bleeding from their branches slows. Persistent dark bleeding from behind the liver suggests injury to the hepatic veins or retrohepatic IVC, which are outside the ligament and drain directly into the systemic circulation.

stem: A 52-year-old man from rural Punjab with cirrhosis due to hepatitis C vomits a large amount of fresh blood. Endoscopy shows oesophageal varices. Which veins form the portal side of the anastomosis that dilates to form these varices?
options: Short gastric veins draining into the splenic vein
explanation: At the lower oesophagus, oesophageal tributaries of the left gastric vein (portal) anastomose with oesophageal veins draining to the azygos system (systemic); portal hypertension dilates this connection into varices. Short gastric veins can contribute to fundal varices, while superior rectal and paraumbilical veins form anorectal and periumbilical anastomoses.

stem: A 23-year-old motorcyclist hits the handlebar and fractures his left 10th and 11th ribs. He is hypotensive and complains of pain at the tip of his left shoulder. Through which nerve is the shoulder pain referred?
explanation: Blood from a ruptured spleen irritates the undersurface of the left hemidiaphragm, whose central part is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5); the pain is referred to the C4 dermatome over the shoulder (Kehr's sign). The intercostal nerves supply the peripheral diaphragm and chest wall, so they explain local rib pain rather than shoulder-tip pain.

stem: A 66-year-old man has painless progressive jaundice, dark urine, pale stools and a palpable, non-tender gallbladder. A CT scan shows a mass. In which part of the pancreas is the mass most likely to be?
explanation: The terminal common bile duct runs in a groove on, or through, the posterior part of the head of the pancreas before joining the main pancreatic duct, so a tumour of the head obstructs it early and causes painless obstructive jaundice. Tumours of the body and tail present later, often with back pain and weight loss.

stem: A 4-year-old boy has painless passage of dark red blood per rectum. A technetium scan shows a focus of uptake in the right lower abdomen. From which embryological structure does the lesion arise?
explanation: A Meckel's diverticulum is a remnant of the vitello-intestinal duct on the antimesenteric border of the ileum, typically about 60 cm from the ileocaecal valve; ectopic gastric mucosa secretes acid and causes ulceration and painless bleeding, which the technetium scan detects. A persistent urachus (from the allantois) connects the bladder to the umbilicus and leaks urine.

stem: A 3-day-old baby has bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. A contrast study shows that the duodenojejunal flexure lies to the right of the midline. Which developmental process has failed?
options: Rotation of the midgut loop around the superior mesenteric artery
Migration of neural crest cells into the bowel wall
explanation: During development the midgut loop herniates into the umbilical cord and rotates 270° anticlockwise around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery as it returns. In malrotation, the duodenojejunal flexure lies to the right and the narrow mesentery predisposes to midgut volvulus, which causes bilious vomiting. Failure of recanalisation causes duodenal atresia, with a normally placed duodenojejunal flexure.

stem: A 1-month-old boy has had constipation and abdominal distension since birth, with delayed passage of meconium. A rectal biopsy is taken. Which finding confirms the most likely diagnosis?
options: Crypt abscesses with depletion of goblet cells in the mucosa
Absence of ganglion cells in the submucosal and myenteric plexuses
explanation: Hirschsprung disease results from failure of neural crest cells to migrate into the distal bowel, so ganglion cells are absent from the submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses and the segment cannot relax. Crypt abscesses suggest ulcerative colitis and villous atrophy suggests coeliac disease.

stem: A 55-year-old man with years of reflux symptoms has an endoscopic biopsy of the lower oesophagus. Which histological change indicates Barrett's oesophagus?
options: Replacement of squamous epithelium by columnar epithelium with goblet cells
Keratinisation of the stratified squamous epithelium
explanation: Barrett's oesophagus is metaplasia of the normal non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium of the lower oesophagus into intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells, a response to chronic acid exposure and a precursor of adenocarcinoma. Eosinophilic infiltration indicates eosinophilic oesophagitis.

stem: A 40-year-old woman has severe colicky right loin pain radiating to the groin. Imaging shows a 4 mm stone in the right ureter. At which site is the ureter narrowest, where small stones most often lodge?
options: Where it crosses the pelvic brim
Where the gonadal vessels cross it
explanation: The ureter has three natural constrictions: the pelviureteric junction, the crossing of the pelvic brim over the iliac vessels, and the vesicoureteric junction, where it passes obliquely through the bladder wall; the vesicoureteric junction is the narrowest and the commonest site of impaction. The gonadal vessels cross the ureter without narrowing it.

stem: During an abdominal hysterectomy, the surgeon clamps the uterine artery close to the lateral fornix of the vagina. Which structure, lying immediately below the artery at this point, is at greatest risk of being clamped or tied?
explanation: About 1.5–2 cm lateral to the cervix, the ureter passes forwards below the uterine artery ('water under the bridge') just above the lateral fornix, so it can be clamped or ligated with the artery. The obturator nerve runs along the lateral pelvic wall, away from the parametrium.

stem: A 10-year-old girl has an ultrasound for recurrent urinary infections, which shows that the lower poles of both kidneys are fused across the midline. Which structure stops the ascent of this fused kidney during development?
explanation: In a horseshoe kidney, the fused lower poles ascend from the pelvis until the isthmus is caught under the inferior mesenteric artery, so the kidneys lie lower than normal. The superior mesenteric artery lies higher and compresses the left renal vein (nutcracker), not the ascending kidney.

stem: A 60-year-old man notices a new left-sided scrotal swelling that feels like a 'bag of worms' and does not collapse when he lies down. A left renal tumour is found. What explains the link between these findings?
options: The left testicular artery arises from the left renal artery
The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein
Lymph from the testis drains to nodes at the renal hilum
The left testicular vein drains directly into the IVC
explanation: The left testicular vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein, so a renal tumour extending into the renal vein can obstruct it and cause a varicocele that persists when supine. The right testicular vein drains directly into the IVC, which is why left varicoceles are commoner. The testicular arteries arise from the aorta.

stem: A woman in the second stage of labour at a THQ hospital is given a pudendal nerve block through the vaginal wall. Which bony landmark is palpated to guide the needle?
explanation: The pudendal nerve passes around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament as it leaves the greater sciatic foramen and enters the lesser sciatic foramen, so the needle is guided transvaginally to just below and medial to the palpable ischial spine. The ischial tuberosity lies more inferiorly and is used for a transperineal approach.

stem: A 32-year-old man falls astride a steel beam. He cannot pass urine, and blood is seen at the external meatus. Over the next day swelling spreads into the scrotum, penis and lower anterior abdominal wall, but not into the thighs. Why does the fluid not extend into the thighs?
options: The superficial perineal fascia (Colles' fascia) is attached to the fascia lata
The urogenital diaphragm blocks downward spread
The deep perineal pouch is closed laterally by the ischial tuberosities
Scarpa's fascia is attached to the inguinal ligament only
explanation: A straddle injury ruptures the bulbar (spongy) urethra, and urine leaks into the superficial perineal pouch beneath Colles' fascia. This fascia is continuous with Scarpa's fascia of the abdominal wall but is attached to the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament and to the ischiopubic rami, so fluid spreads to the scrotum, penis and abdominal wall but not into the thighs.

stem: A 68-year-old man with a raised PSA has a hard nodule felt on digital rectal examination. In which zone of the prostate do most carcinomas arise?
explanation: About 70 % of prostate cancers arise in the peripheral zone, which lies posteriorly and laterally and is therefore palpable on rectal examination. Benign prostatic hyperplasia arises mainly in the transition zone around the urethra, which is why it causes urinary symptoms early.

stem: A 35-year-old man notices bright red blood on the toilet paper after defecation but has no pain. Proctoscopy shows internal haemorrhoids. Why are internal haemorrhoids usually painless?
options: They contain no nerve fibres at all
They are above the pectinate line, which has autonomic (visceral) innervation
They are covered by keratinised squamous epithelium
They are supplied by the inferior rectal nerve
explanation: Above the pectinate line the anal canal is lined by columnar mucosa with visceral (autonomic) innervation, insensitive to pain from cutting or pricking, so internal haemorrhoids bleed painlessly. Below the line the canal is supplied by the somatic inferior rectal nerve, which is why external haemorrhoids and fissures are very painful.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has severe lower abdominal pain, a positive pregnancy test and signs of internal bleeding. Ultrasound shows free fluid in the pelvis. In which part of the peritoneal cavity does blood first collect when she is upright?
explanation: The rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in the upright female, so blood from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy collects there first; it lies behind the posterior vaginal fornix. The hepatorenal pouch is the lowest point when the patient is supine.

stem: A 63-year-old man has an abscess in the ischioanal fossa beside the anal canal. While draining it, the surgeon avoids the lateral wall of the fossa. Which structures run in a fascial canal on this wall?
options: Pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels
explanation: The pudendal (Alcock's) canal is a split in the obturator internus fascia on the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa, carrying the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels. The obturator nerve leaves the pelvis through the obturator canal higher up, above the pelvic floor.

stem: A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation develops left-sided abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea. Colonoscopy shows ischaemic colitis most marked near the splenic flexure. Why is this region particularly vulnerable to ischaemia?
options: It is supplied only by the inferior phrenic artery
It is the watershed between the superior and inferior mesenteric artery territories
Its veins drain directly into the systemic circulation
explanation: The splenic flexure lies at the junction of the territories of the middle colic (superior mesenteric) and left colic (inferior mesenteric) arteries, where the marginal artery may be thin or discontinuous, so it suffers first when perfusion falls. The colon there drains into the portal system like the rest of the colon.

stem: A 50-year-old woman has a gastrectomy for gastric cancer. Two years later she has a macrocytic anaemia with glossitis. Loss of which gastric cells explains this?
explanation: Parietal cells of the gastric body and fundus secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, which is needed to absorb vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum; after gastrectomy B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia once liver stores run out. Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, and G cells in the antrum secrete gastrin.

stem: A 6-week-old boy has projectile non-bilious vomiting after every feed and a small olive-shaped mass in the right upper abdomen. Which layer is hypertrophied?
explanation: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis results from hypertrophy of the circular smooth muscle of the pyloric sphincter, which narrows the outlet and forms the palpable 'olive'; it is treated by pyloromyotomy, dividing the muscle down to the mucosa. The vomiting is non-bilious because the obstruction is proximal to the ampulla of Vater.

stem: A cardiology trainee is placing a catheter into the coronary sinus. Into which chamber does the coronary sinus open?
explanation: The coronary sinus runs in the posterior atrioventricular groove and opens into the right atrium between the opening of the IVC and the tricuspid orifice, returning most of the venous blood of the heart. It does not open into the left atrium in normal anatomy.

stem: A 57-year-old man has a lateral wall myocardial infarction with ST elevation in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6. Which artery, running in the left atrioventricular groove, is most likely occluded?
explanation: The left circumflex artery runs in the left part of the atrioventricular (coronary) groove around to the back of the heart and supplies the lateral wall of the left ventricle through its marginal branches. The LAD runs in the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the anterior wall and septum.

stem: Where on the chest wall is the aortic valve area for auscultation?
options: Right second intercostal space next to the sternum
Left second intercostal space next to the sternum
Left fourth intercostal space next to the sternum
Left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line
explanation: Aortic valve sounds are conducted along the ascending aorta and are best heard in the right second intercostal space at the sternal edge. The left second space is the pulmonary area, and the fifth space in the midclavicular line is the mitral area.

stem: During radiofrequency ablation, an electrophysiologist works in the triangle of Koch in the right atrium. Which structure lies at the apex of this triangle and must be protected?
explanation: The triangle of Koch, bounded by the tendon of Todaro, the septal cusp of the tricuspid valve and the opening of the coronary sinus, contains the atrioventricular node near its apex; damage causes heart block. The sinoatrial node lies at the upper end of the crista terminalis near the SVC opening.

stem: A 30-year-old man with a stab wound to the chest has hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure and muffled heart sounds. Between which layers does blood accumulate in cardiac tamponade?
options: Fibrous pericardium and parietal serous pericardium
Parietal and visceral layers of serous pericardium
explanation: The pericardial cavity is the potential space between the parietal serous layer (fused to the fibrous pericardium) and the visceral serous layer (epicardium); blood there compresses the heart because the fibrous pericardium cannot stretch acutely. There is no space between the fibrous pericardium and its parietal serous lining.

stem: A 2-month-old baby in Quetta has a loud pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. Echocardiography shows a ventricular septal defect. Which part of the interventricular septum is most commonly defective?
options: Inlet part beside the tricuspid valve
Outlet part below the pulmonary valve
explanation: Most ventricular septal defects involve the membranous (perimembranous) septum, the thin upper part formed from endocardial cushion tissue and the bulbar ridges, the last part of the septum to close. Muscular defects are the next commonest and often close spontaneously.

stem: A cyanosed newborn is found to have the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk from the left ventricle. Which embryological error causes this?
options: The aorticopulmonary septum develops without spiralling
Anterior displacement of the infundibular septum
Persistence of the truncus arteriosus without any septum
explanation: Normally the aorticopulmonary septum spirals as it divides the truncus arteriosus and conus, so the aorta connects to the left ventricle; if it develops straight, the great arteries are transposed. Failure of the septum to form at all leaves a single persistent truncus arteriosus over a VSD.

stem: A paediatric surgeon divides a fibrous cord running in the free edge of the falciform ligament from the umbilicus to the liver. Which fetal vessel does this cord represent?
explanation: The left umbilical vein carried oxygenated blood from the placenta to the liver and becomes the ligamentum teres hepatis in the free edge of the falciform ligament. The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum, and the umbilical arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments.

stem: A doctor hears crackles in front of the right chest between the fourth and sixth costal cartilages near the sternum. Which lobe of the lung is mainly heard at this site?
explanation: The horizontal fissure of the right lung follows the fourth costal cartilage, and the oblique fissure reaches the sixth costal cartilage anteriorly, so the right middle lobe lies between them at the front. The lower lobe is heard mainly from the back, and the lingula is part of the left upper lobe.

stem: A 55-year-old man in the medical ward has a small pleural effusion. When he stands, where does the fluid first collect?
explanation: The costodiaphragmatic recess is the lowest part of the pleural cavity, between the costal and diaphragmatic pleura, so fluid gathers there first and blunts the costophrenic angle on an upright X-ray. The costomediastinal recess lies anteriorly behind the sternum.

stem: A baby born at 28 weeks develops respiratory distress shortly after birth. Deficiency of a substance produced by which cells explains the condition?
explanation: Type II pneumocytes produce surfactant, which lowers alveolar surface tension and prevents collapse at end-expiration; production is inadequate before about 34 weeks, causing neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Type I pneumocytes are thin cells for gas exchange and do not secrete surfactant.

stem: A newborn drools excessively and chokes and becomes cyanosed during the first feed. A nasogastric tube cannot be passed beyond 10 cm, and air is seen in the stomach on X-ray. Which anatomical arrangement is most likely?
options: Isolated oesophageal atresia without a fistula
Atresia with a fistula from the upper pouch only
Oesophageal atresia with a fistula from the trachea to the distal oesophagus
explanation: The commonest type (about 85 %) is a blind upper oesophageal pouch with a fistula between the trachea and the lower oesophagus; the tube coils in the pouch and air passes through the fistula into the stomach. Isolated atresia without a fistula gives a gasless abdomen, and an H-type fistula allows a tube to pass.

stem: From which spinal nerve roots does the phrenic nerve arise?
explanation: The phrenic nerve arises mainly from C4 with contributions from C3 and C5 and is the sole motor supply to the diaphragm. This explains why high cervical cord injuries above C3 cause respiratory paralysis.

stem: A CT scan of a patient with SVC obstruction shows a large collateral vein arching over the root of the right lung to enter the superior vena cava. Which vein is this?
explanation: The azygos vein ascends on the right of the vertebral bodies and arches forwards over the root of the right lung at about T4 to drain into the posterior aspect of the SVC; it becomes an important collateral in caval obstruction. The hemiazygos vein lies on the left and drains into the azygos.

stem: The deep inguinal ring is the start of the inguinal canal. In which layer of the abdominal wall is it an opening?
explanation: The deep inguinal ring is an opening in the transversalis fascia just above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; the fascia continues along the cord as the internal spermatic fascia. The superficial ring is an opening in the external oblique aponeurosis.

stem: In a female, which structure passes through the inguinal canal?
explanation: In women the inguinal canal carries the round ligament of the uterus, which ends in the labium majus, together with the ilioinguinal nerve. The ovarian ligament joins the ovary to the uterus and stays within the pelvis.

stem: A 2-year-old boy has a swelling in the right side of the scrotum that becomes larger during the day and smaller overnight. It transilluminates. Persistence of which structure explains it?
explanation: A patent processus vaginalis allows peritoneal fluid to pass into the tunica vaginalis, producing a communicating hydrocele that varies in size; a wider patency allows an indirect inguinal hernia. The gubernaculum guides testicular descent and becomes the scrotal ligament, and a patent urachus leaks urine at the umbilicus.

stem: Which dermatome includes the skin around the umbilicus?
explanation: The umbilicus lies in the T10 dermatome; T6 is near the xiphoid process and L1 covers the groin just above the inguinal ligament. This is useful for localising spinal cord lesions and understanding referred pain from midgut structures.

stem: A surgeon making a lower midline incision notes that below a certain curved line, midway between the umbilicus and the pubic symphysis, rectus abdominis lies directly on the transversalis fascia. What change in the rectus sheath occurs at this arcuate line?
options: The aponeuroses of all three flat muscles pass in front of rectus
The external oblique aponeurosis passes behind rectus
The internal oblique aponeurosis splits around rectus
explanation: Above the arcuate line the internal oblique aponeurosis splits around rectus, and transversus abdominis joins the posterior layer; below the line all three aponeuroses pass in front of rectus, leaving only transversalis fascia behind it. The inferior epigastric vessels enter the sheath at this line.

stem: A 60-year-old man has haematemesis from a bleeding gastric ulcer high on the lesser curvature. Which artery is most likely to be the source?
explanation: The left gastric artery, from the coeliac trunk, runs along the upper lesser curvature between the layers of the lesser omentum, so an ulcer there may erode it. The right gastroepiploic artery runs along the greater curvature, and the gastroduodenal artery is related to posterior duodenal ulcers.

stem: A surgeon passes a finger into the epiploic foramen (opening into the lesser sac). Which structure lies in front of the finger?
options: Hepatoduodenal ligament containing the portal triad
explanation: The epiploic foramen is bounded in front by the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) containing the bile duct, hepatic artery and portal vein; behind it lies the IVC, above it the caudate lobe and below it the first part of the duodenum. This relationship is used in the Pringle manoeuvre.

stem: A 48-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has dilated tortuous veins radiating from the umbilicus. Which veins on the portal side form this anastomosis?
explanation: Caput medusae results when the paraumbilical veins, running with the ligamentum teres from the left portal vein, dilate and connect with systemic superficial veins of the abdominal wall around the umbilicus. The superficial and inferior epigastric veins are the systemic side of the anastomosis.

stem: A 42-year-old woman with right upper quadrant pain has tenderness where the right linea semilunaris meets the costal margin, and she catches her breath on inspiration when this point is pressed. Which organ lies under this landmark?
options: Upper pole of the right kidney
explanation: The fundus of the gallbladder lies at the tip of the right ninth costal cartilage, where the lateral border of rectus (linea semilunaris) meets the costal margin; inspiration brings an inflamed gallbladder down against the examining hand (Murphy's sign). The pancreatic head lies deeper and more medial, at about L1–L2.

stem: Gastrointestinal bleeding is classified as upper or lower according to whether its source is above or below a particular landmark. Which landmark is this?
explanation: Bleeding proximal to the duodenojejunal flexure, suspended by the suspensory muscle (ligament of Treitz), is classed as upper GI bleeding, and distal bleeding as lower. The ampulla of Vater lies in the second part of the duodenum, well within the upper tract.

stem: A histology slide of the small intestine shows large aggregates of lymphoid follicles in the mucosa and submucosa on the antimesenteric side. Which part of the gut is this?
explanation: Peyer's patches, large aggregated lymphoid follicles, are characteristic of the ileum; they are the site of invasion and ulceration in typhoid fever, which can perforate. The duodenum is identified by Brunner's glands in the submucosa, and the jejunum by tall villi and prominent circular folds without large patches.

stem: A 2-day-old baby with Down syndrome has bilious vomiting. Surgery shows a ring of pancreatic tissue encircling the second part of the duodenum. Abnormal development of which structure causes this?
explanation: The ventral pancreatic bud normally rotates behind the duodenum to fuse with the dorsal bud; if part of it (often bifid) passes around both sides of the duodenum, an annular pancreas forms and may obstruct the second part. The dorsal bud forms most of the body and tail and does not encircle the duodenum.

stem: During a left nephrectomy, the surgeon identifies structures at the renal hilum. In what order, from anterior to posterior, do the main structures usually lie?
options: Renal artery, renal vein, renal pelvis
Renal pelvis, renal artery, renal vein
Renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis
Renal vein, renal pelvis, renal artery
explanation: At the hilum the renal vein lies most anteriorly, the renal artery in between and the renal pelvis most posteriorly (VAP), although branches of the artery may also pass behind the pelvis. This order guides hilar dissection and explains why the vein is met first from the front.

stem: A surgeon performing a right adrenalectomy for phaeochromocytoma takes particular care with the right adrenal vein. Why is this vein especially hazardous?
options: It drains into the right renal vein after a long course
It runs inside the right crus of the diaphragm
It is very short and drains directly into the inferior vena cava
It passes in front of the duodenum
explanation: The right suprarenal vein is very short and enters the posterior surface of the IVC directly, so traction can tear the IVC and cause serious bleeding. The left suprarenal vein is longer and drains into the left renal vein.

stem: During a pelvic operation, the surgeon traces the ureter as it enters the pelvis. Which vessel does the ureter cross at the pelvic brim?
options: Bifurcation of the common iliac artery
Origin of the inferior mesenteric artery
explanation: The ureter enters the pelvis by crossing the bifurcation of the common iliac artery (or the start of the external iliac artery) at the pelvic brim, a narrow point where stones lodge and where it is identified at surgery. The inferior mesenteric artery arises much higher at L3.

stem: A pathology student examines a biopsy of the urinary bladder. Which epithelium normally lines it?
explanation: The bladder, ureters and renal pelvis are lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), whose surface umbrella cells flatten as the bladder fills; most bladder cancers are urothelial carcinomas. Squamous metaplasia can occur with chronic irritation such as schistosomiasis, but it is not normal.

stem: A 25-year-old man has a pelvic fracture in a road traffic accident. He cannot void, there is blood at the meatus, and on rectal examination the prostate is 'high-riding'. Which part of the urethra is most likely ruptured?
explanation: In pelvic fractures the puboprostatic ligaments and pelvic floor are disrupted, and the membranous urethra is sheared at the prostatic apex, letting the prostate rise; urine extravasates into the retropubic space. Bulbar urethral rupture follows straddle injuries, with urine spreading into the scrotum and penis.

stem: A gynaecologist needs to aspirate fluid from the rectouterine pouch in a woman with suspected ectopic pregnancy. Through which part of the vagina is the needle passed?
options: Lower third of the anterior wall
explanation: The posterior vaginal fornix is covered directly by the peritoneum of the rectouterine pouch, so a needle passed through it (culdocentesis) enters the pouch. The anterior fornix is related to the vesicouterine pouch and bladder, and the lateral fornix to the ureter and uterine vessels.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with several vaginal deliveries has uterine prolapse. Which ligaments provide the main ligamentous support to the cervix and are weakened in this condition?
explanation: The transverse cervical (cardinal) ligaments, with the uterosacral ligaments and the levator ani, are the main supports of the uterus and vaginal vault. The round ligaments keep the uterus anteverted but give little support against prolapse, and the broad ligaments are folds of peritoneum.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with an ovarian cyst that has twisted complains of pain spreading down the medial side of her thigh. Irritation of which nerve, lying on the lateral pelvic wall next to the ovary, explains this?
explanation: The ovary lies in the ovarian fossa on the lateral pelvic wall, close to the obturator nerve, which supplies the skin of the medial thigh; inflammation or a mass can irritate the nerve and refer pain there. The genitofemoral nerve lies on psoas and supplies the upper anterior thigh and genital area.

stem: A 28-year-old man has a testicular tumour. To which lymph nodes does it spread first?
explanation: The testis develops on the posterior abdominal wall and descends with its vessels and lymphatics, so its lymph drains to the para-aortic nodes around the origin of the testicular arteries at about L1–L2. The scrotal skin, by contrast, drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

stem: A 50-year-old man has a squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal below the pectinate line. Which lymph nodes should be examined first for spread?
explanation: Below the pectinate line the anal canal is derived from the proctodeum (ectoderm), and its lymph drains to the superficial inguinal nodes; above the line it drains to the internal iliac and inferior mesenteric nodes. This is why inguinal nodes are palpated in anal cancer.

stem: A 45-year-old man has a long-standing ulcer high on the posterior wall of the body of the stomach that erodes into the vessel lying behind it, causing massive bleeding. Which artery is most likely affected?
explanation: The splenic artery runs tortuously along the upper border of the pancreas in the bed of the stomach, behind the lesser sac, so a penetrating posterior gastric ulcer may erode it. The right gastric artery runs along the lower lesser curvature near the pylorus.

stem: An embryology tutor explains that the foregut, midgut and hindgut are each supplied by one unpaired branch of the aorta. Which artery supplies the midgut?
explanation: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, from the second part of the duodenum (below the major papilla) to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. The coeliac trunk supplies the foregut, and the inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut.

stem: In an adult male, the digital rectal examination is used to assess the prostate. On which wall of the rectum is the prostate felt?
explanation: The prostate lies in front of the rectum, separated by the rectovesical (Denonvilliers') fascia, so it is palpated through the anterior rectal wall. The sacrum and coccyx are felt posteriorly.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is stabbed below the right costal margin in the midclavicular line. Which intraperitoneal organ is most likely to be injured at this site?
explanation: The liver occupies the right hypochondrium and extends below the right costal margin, so penetrating wounds there commonly injure it, along with the gallbladder. The pancreas is retroperitoneal and deep, and the spleen lies in the left upper quadrant.
